title: Slavery, Freedom, and the Struggle for Empire
summary: The eighteenth century joined an expanding rhetoric of British liberty to the peak of the Atlantic slave trade. Triangular trade routes carried manufactured goods, captives, and plantation staples around the ocean, with the brutal Middle Passage killing about one in five Africans in transit. Although under 5 percent of all enslaved Africans landed in mainland North America, three distinct slave systems took hold there: tobacco plantations in the Chesapeake, rice and indigo plantations in South Carolina and Georgia worked under the task system, and smaller-scale nonplantation slavery in the northern colonies. Out of many African peoples, enslaved men and women forged new African-American cultures blending African, European, and American elements, and they resisted bondage by running away and, occasionally, in armed risings like the 1739 Stono Rebellion.

Free colonists, meanwhile, absorbed Britain's self-image as the world's freest nation. Republicanism prized public virtue and property-holding independence, while Lockean liberalism grounded government in a social contract protecting natural rights. Under salutary neglect, elected assemblies grew assertive, and a broad white male franchise, an expanding press, the Zenger verdict of 1735, Enlightenment rationalism, and the emotional revivals of the Great Awakening led by Edwards and Whitefield all widened the public sphere and taught ordinary colonists to question established authority.

Britain's rivals fared poorly by comparison: Spain's borderlands from Florida to Texas and the California missions of Junipero Serra remained thinly settled, and New France, though vast, was underpopulated. Rivalry over the Ohio Valley ignited the Seven Years' War in 1754, and Britain's victory in the 1763 Peace of Paris expelled France from North America. The triumph left Indians without the leverage of playing empires against each other, sparking Pontiac's Rebellion, inspired partly by the prophet Neolin, and Britain's Proclamation of 1763 barring settlement beyond the Appalachians, a restriction colonists resented. Wartime debts and these frontier tensions set the stage for the imperial crisis to come.
big_ideas: The eighteenth century saw freedom and slavery expand together: Britain celebrated liberty while its merchants dominated the Atlantic slave trade.
Three regional slave systems, Chesapeake tobacco, Lower South rice, and northern nonplantation slavery, produced distinct African-American cultures and forms of resistance.
Republicanism (public virtue and independence) and liberalism (natural rights and the social contract) supplied the era's key languages of freedom.
Salutary neglect allowed colonial assemblies to grow powerful, and a wide white male franchise, a booming press, and the Zenger trial expanded the public sphere.
The Enlightenment elevated reason and science, while the Great Awakening's revivals democratized religion and encouraged ordinary people to judge elites for themselves.
Britain's victory in the Seven Years' War drove France from North America, transformed the global balance of power, and saddled Britain with debts it would try to recover from the colonies.
The French withdrawal stripped Indians of balance-of-power diplomacy, provoking Pontiac's Rebellion and the Proclamation of 1763, which angered land-hungry colonists.

key_terms.def: The Atlantic crossing endured by enslaved Africans, the middle leg of the triangular trade, in which people were packed into ship holds and roughly 20 percent died before reaching America.
Enslaved African who bought his freedom and published a widely read 1789 autobiography attacking slavery and the notion of African inferiority.
Labor arrangement on South Carolina and Georgia rice plantations assigning each slave a daily quota, after which time belonged to the worker, unlike the supervised gang labor of the Chesapeake.
1739 uprising in which South Carolina slaves, many Kongo-born, seized weapons and marched toward Spanish Florida shouting 'Liberty'; its suppression brought a harsher slave code.
Political outlook holding that liberty depended on active civic participation by economically independent, virtuous citizens willing to put the public good above self-interest.
Lockean philosophy locating freedom in individual natural rights and a social contract that limits government's power over private life, property, and conscience.
English philosopher whose Two Treatises of Government argued that legitimate authority rests on consent and that people may resist rulers who violate their natural rights.
Britain's informal early-eighteenth-century practice of loosely enforcing colonial regulations, which allowed American assemblies to claim ever-greater control over local affairs.
1735 New York libel case in which a jury acquitted printer John Peter Zenger for attacks on the governor, strengthening the popular idea that publishing the truth should be protected.
Transatlantic intellectual movement applying reason and the scientific method to society and religion; American Deists like Franklin saw God's design in natural law rather than revelation.

Emotional religious revivals of the 1730s-1740s, spread by Jonathan Edwards and the touring evangelist George Whitefield, that split churches, spawned new denominations, and encouraged independent judgment.
Franciscan friar who founded California's first mission at San Diego in 1769; his mission system converted thousands of Indians but relied on forced labor and contributed to steep population decline.

key_terms.term: Seven Years' War (French and Indian War)
key_terms.def: Global Anglo-French conflict beginning in America in 1754 over the Ohio Valley; Britain's victory, sealed by the 1763 Peace of Paris, ended French power in North America.
Benjamin Franklin's 1754 proposal for a Grand Council of colonial delegates to manage defense, taxation, and Indian affairs; colonial assemblies rejected it to protect their own power.
1763 pan-Indian assault on British forts in the Ohio Valley and Great Lakes, inspired partly by the Delaware prophet Neolin's call to reject European goods and reclaim independence.
Royal order closing lands west of the Appalachians to colonial settlement and private purchase, meant to calm the frontier but deeply resented by settlers and speculators.

timeline.event: The Act of Union joins England and Scotland to form Great Britain.
Enslaved people stage the century's first slave uprising in New York City.
The French found New Orleans, anchoring Louisiana and the Mississippi Valley trade.
Georgia is chartered under James Oglethorpe, initially banning slavery.
A jury acquits printer John Peter Zenger of seditious libel in New York.
The Stono Rebellion erupts in South Carolina; George Whitefield begins his American revival tour.
Rumors of a slave conspiracy set off a panic and executions in New York City.
Fighting begins in the Ohio Valley and Franklin's Albany Plan of Union is rejected.
The Seven Years' War formally begins, spreading the Anglo-French struggle worldwide.
The Peace of Paris ends French rule in North America; Pontiac's Rebellion breaks out and Britain issues the Proclamation of 1763.
The Paxton Boys march on Philadelphia after massacring Conestoga Indians, ending Pennsylvania's era of peaceful Indian relations.
Father Junipero Serra establishes Spain's first California mission at San Diego.

themes: Work, exchange, and technology: The Atlantic slave trade and plantation staples like tobacco, rice, and sugar powered imperial commerce and even helped finance Britain's industrialization.
American and national identity: African-American cultures formed out of diverse African origins, while free colonists built identities around British liberty, republicanism, and Protestantism.
Politics and power: Salutary neglect, rising assemblies, an expanding press, and the Great Awakening all diffused authority downward and prepared colonists to challenge imperial control.
America in the world: The Seven Years' War was a global contest whose outcome redrew empires, burdened Britain with debt, and pushed the colonies toward crisis.
Migration and geography: Contests over the Ohio Valley, the Proclamation Line, and Spanish borderland missions show how control of western land shaped relations among empires, settlers, and Indians.
